turns.content: I founded the Saturday Morning Mending Circle at Elmridge Community Hall about two years ago. It started with three older women who wanted a quiet place to repair things and talk without feeling judged. Last weekend a father named Greg asked if he and his teenage son could come learn denim repair. I felt this immediate protective panic, then immediate guilt for feeling that way. Am I wrong to hesitate?

You’re not wrong to hesitate. That flash of panic, then the guilt stacking on top of it, is a pretty honest reaction for someone who built a small, quiet room and suddenly got asked to change the lock.

What you started wasn’t a public drop-in sewing class. It was three older women who wanted a place to repair things *and* talk without feeling judged. Two years in, that container has a texture: pace, privacy, who gets to be unguarded. A father and a teenage son walking in doesn’t have to be a threat for it to still be a *change*. New people change a small group even when they’re kind, curious, and there for denim.

The guilt is doing a different job. It’s the part of you that knows mending is for everyone, that a dad teaching his kid to patch jeans is actually lovely, and that “this space isn’t for you” can sound like a door slammed for the wrong reasons. Those two feelings can sit next to each other without one of them making you a villain.

A useful split:

- **The craft** can be shared.
- **This Saturday morning circle** doesn’t have to become the vehicle for every good request.

Hesitation is you noticing that if Greg and his son become regulars, the original women may stop saying the things they came there to say. That’s stewardship, not a character assassination of Greg.

Some ways through that don’t force a yes/no on the spot:

- Ask the original members, plainly: “A dad and his teenage son want to learn denim repair. Does that still feel like our Saturday, or do we want a different hour for that?”
- Offer a one-off skill share — “come for an hour, we’ll show you a patch, then the circle goes back to itself” — instead of an open membership.
- Keep Saturday as the quiet circle and start a separate “learn to mend” slot if you actually *want* the teaching part.

You’re allowed to protect a room that was built so people wouldn’t feel judged. You’re also allowed to be glad a kid wants to learn this. The mistake would be treating the panic as proof you’re cruel, or treating the guilt as proof you have to say yes.

Thanks for that. It helps to hear the panic and the guilt don't cancel each other out.

Martha was widowed last spring. She told me once this was the only place she could cry without someone trying to fix it. I don't want to lose that for her.

That detail about Martha is the whole argument, really. Not “men bad.” Not “teenagers ruin crafts.” She named the actual job of the room: she can fall apart there and nobody will tidy her up.

A dad and a teenage son don’t have to do anything wrong for that to disappear. Grief gets quieter when the audience changes. People start performing okay-ness. Someone offers a tissue too fast, or a pep talk, or just *watches*. Martha already told you this is the only place that doesn’t do that. You’re allowed to treat that as load-bearing.

Protecting it doesn’t mean you have to make Greg the villain, and it also doesn’t mean you have to put Martha on a committee about whether Greg is allowed in. Don’t make her the public reason. That’s a second job she didn’t ask for.

What you can do is hold the original contract:

Saturday morning stays the quiet circle. Same people, same pace, same permission to cry into a sock heel.

If you want to be generous to Greg, that’s a different hour, a different day, or a one-time “here’s how you patch jeans” demo that is clearly *teaching*, not *joining*.

You’re not choosing denim over a kid. You’re choosing not to turn Martha’s last unfixed place into a family workshop. That’s not panic. That’s you remembering why the three of them showed up in the first place.

That split between teaching and joining makes sense. I've been thinking about what to actually say to Greg. If I offer a separate workshop, how do I explain it without making him feel like they're being excluded?

Lead with the yes on the *request*, not the no on Saturday. He asked to learn denim repair with his son. That’s the thing you can be genuinely glad about. Saturday morning is a different thing: a small, ongoing circle that already has a shape. If you say that plainly, it lands as matching, not as “you two don’t belong.”

Don’t mention Martha. Don’t mention crying. Don’t over-explain gender. Extra justification is what makes people feel politely ejected.

Something like this, out loud or in a message:

“I’m really glad you asked — denim repair with your son is a great thing to learn together. Saturday morning isn’t actually a drop-in class, though. It’s a small group that’s been meeting for a couple of years, more like a quiet regular circle than a workshop.

What I *can* do is set up a separate session that’s actually for teaching. You and your son would be welcome there, and I’ll walk you through a solid denim patch. If that sounds good, I can look at a time that isn’t Saturday morning and get back to you.”

That’s the whole move: his ask is welcome, this hour isn’t the format for it, here’s the format that is.

A few things that help it not feel like a brush-off:

- Offer a real next step, not a vague “sometime.” Even “let me check the hall calendar this week” is better than “maybe we could do a workshop.”
- Sound like you mean the workshop. If it feels like a consolation prize, he’ll hear that.
- Keep it short. Once you’ve named the circle vs. the class, stop talking.

If he pushes — “couldn’t we just sit in one Saturday?” — you can stay kind and still hold the line:

“I get why that’d be simpler, but that morning really isn’t set up as a teaching hour, and I want to keep it that way for the people who already rely on it. I’d rather do right by you two in a session that’s actually for learning.”

You’re not telling him he’s excluded from mending. You’re telling him Saturday isn’t a class, and you’re willing to make one. That’s a fair, adult distinction.

That script is clear, and I appreciate having actual words to say.

One worry still sits with me. If I offer a separate session, I'll be the one running it. More booking, more supplies, more time. Is it fair to feel annoyed about that extra work on top of protecting Saturday?

Yes. Protecting Saturday and becoming Greg’s unpaid instructor are two different jobs. Feeling annoyed about the second one is completely fair.

The separate session was a *possible* kindness, not the price of keeping the circle intact. You can hold Saturday as it is and still not add booking, supplies, and another slot to your week. “No, this isn’t a class, and I’m not starting one” is a complete answer.

Annoyance here is useful. It’s you noticing that the compromise quietly turned into *you* absorbing the cost so nobody else has to feel disappointed. That’s a fast way to resent a perfectly decent dad who only asked a question.

You have more options than “run a workshop” or “let them into Saturday”:

- Thank him, decline Saturday, and don’t offer a replacement. “I don’t have capacity to teach a separate session, but I’m glad you’re learning this with your son.”
- Point him somewhere that already exists — a library program, a repair café, a YouTube demo, another mender who actually *likes* teaching.
- If you do want to help once, make it finite: one hour, one patch, no ongoing class, no new standing commitment.

You’re allowed to protect Martha’s room *and* protect your own time. Greg asked for access to a skill. He didn’t ask you to build a second institution around that ask. The guilt can wait in the hallway.

That's the part I hadn't let myself say. That offering a separate session means I'm the one who absorbs the work. I think I needed to hear it's okay to just decline Saturday and not build something else.

Yeah. That’s the piece that was getting dressed up as generosity.

Declining Saturday doesn’t create a debt you have to pay off with a second event. You can just not add the work. Greg asked a question. “This isn’t a class, and I’m not starting one” is a full answer.

The circle already has a job. So do you. Neither of those jobs is “make sure a reasonable request never has to hear no.”

If you want words that don’t over-explain:

“I’m glad you and your son want to learn denim repair. Saturday morning isn’t a teaching session, though, and I don’t have the capacity to run a separate one. I hope you find a good way to learn it together.”

That’s it. No workshop, no apology tour, no extra calendar. You get to keep the room as it is, and you get to keep your time. Both of those are allowed.
